title: How To Avoid Labeling Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that difficult students already feel different from their classmates, and that much common well-meaning advice for helping them actually reinforces the label of 'difficult' or 'behavior problem.' He lists five practices to stop: pulling students aside for pep-talks, using proximity to control them, fussing over them with frequent check-ins and praise, using behavior contracts, and holding private negative thoughts about them that inevitably surface. Each practice, he argues, communicates to the student and the class that this student is fundamentally different and less capable, which becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The proposed remedy is to change the story students tell about themselves by treating them like a regular member of the class—same accountability, same warmth, same trust—so they begin behaving like a regular member of the class. The article closes with a direct call for teachers to be the one adult who finally changes a difficult student's trajectory.
points: Difficult students already feel different from peers, and Linsin argues common 'helpful' interventions actually reinforce that label.
Five practices are named to stop: pulling students aside for pep-talks, using proximity control, fussing over them, behavior contracts, and privately negative thinking.
These practices are said to create a self-fulfilling prophecy in which students internalize the belief that they're incapable of self-control.
The remedy is to 'change the story' by treating the student as a regular class member with the same accountability, warmth, and trust as everyone else.
The article frames teachers as capable of being the one adult who interrupts a difficult student's negative trajectory and changes their life.
quotes: Difficult students feel different from their classmates. As if, they don’t quite fit in.
And yet, the most common advice given to teachers to help these students only makes matters worse.

It’s common for teachers to pull difficult students aside to cajole, pep-talk , and otherwise try to convince them to behave. But the deeper and far stronger message they get from you is that they’re not like all the rest, who you don’t pull aside.
Nothing tells a student they’re different and less able than a behavior contract.
These efforts to improve behavior, which many difficult students have been subject to for years and years, merely strengthen the limiting beliefs they have about themselves.
Be the one teacher to say “Enough is enough, and I believe in you.” Create a new prophecy for them to fulfill.
